entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4629"/><div sID="gen6713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4629"/><hi type="bold">8. spreadeth out--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Is 40:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>). But throughout it is not so much God's creating, as His governing, power over nature that is set forth. A storm seems a struggle between Nature and her Lord! Better, therefore, "Who boweth the heavens alone," without help of any other. God descends from the bowed-down heaven to the earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Psa 18:9</reference>). The storm, wherein the clouds descend, suggests this image. In the descent of the vault of heaven, God has come down from His high throne and walks majestically over the mountain waves (Hebrew, "heights"), as a conqueror taming their violence. So "tread upon" (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">De 33:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">Am 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.14.26">Mt 14:26</reference>). The Egyptian hieroglyphic for impossibility is a man walking on waves. <div eID="gen6713" type="x-p"/>

The Chaldeans and Arabs, early named the stars and grouped them in constellations; often travelling and tending flocks by night, they would naturally do so, especially as the rise and setting of some stars mark the distinction of seasons. Brinkley, presuming the stars here mentioned to be those of Taurus and Scorpio, and that these were the cardinal constellations of spring and autumn in Job's time, calculates, by the precession of equinoxes, the time of Job to be eight hundred eighteen years after the deluge, and one hundred eighty-four before Abraham.<div eID="gen6715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Orion--</hi>Hebrew, "the fool"; in <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">Job 38:31</reference> he appears fettered with "bands." I see him not: he passeth on--</hi>The image is that of a howling wind (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Is 21:1</reference>). Umbreit takes these as the words of God, translating, "What availeth the might of the strong?" "Here (saith he) behold! what availeth justice? Who will appoint me a time to plead?" (So <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jr 49:19</reference>). The last words certainly apply better to God than to Job. The sense is substantially the same if we make "me" apply to Job. The "lo!" expresses God's swift readiness for battle when challenged. <div eID="gen6727" type="x-p"/>

If--</hi>Rather, "While (His) scourge slays suddenly (the wicked, <reference osisRef="Job.9.22">Job 9:22</reference>), He laughs at (disregards; not derides) the pining away of the innocent." The only difference, says Job, between the innocent and guilty is, the latter are slain by a sudden stroke, the former pine away gradually. The translation, "trial," does not express the antithesis to "slay suddenly," as "pining away" does [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6731" type="x-p"/>

The only difference, says Job, between the innocent and guilty is, the latter are slain by a sudden stroke, the former pine away gradually. The translation, "trial," does not express the antithesis to "slay suddenly," as "pining away" does [Umbreit].

In the wide Persian empire such couriers, on dromedaries or on foot, were employed to carry the royal commands to the distant provinces (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.13">Es 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.3.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.8.14">8:14</reference>). "My days" are not like the slow caravan, but the fleet post. The "days" are themselves poetically said to "see no good," instead of Job in them (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.10">1Pe 3:10</reference>). <div eID="gen6734" type="x-p"/>

The "if" is better omitted; I (am treated by God as) wicked; why then labor I in vain (to disprove His charge)? <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4650"/><div sID="gen6741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4650"/><hi type="bold">33. daysman--</hi>"mediator," or "umpire"; the imposition of whose hand expresses power to adjudicate between the persons. There might be one on a level with Job, the one party; but Job knew of none on a level with the Almighty, the other party (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.25">1Sa 2:25</reference>). We Christians know of such a Mediator (not, however, in the sense of umpire) on a level with both--the God-man, Christ Jesus (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>). <div eID="gen6741" type="x-p"/>
